stops.name: Playa Las Coloradas, the landing in the swamp
stops.campa: At dawn on the second of December the Granma grounds on a mudbank a mile short of solid Cuba, and the invasion wades ashore through two hours of mangrove swamp, losing weapons, food and boots to the black water. Batista's planes are already hunting. A comrade calls it not a landing but a shipwreck, and the canon keeps the phrase because it is exact. Eighty-two exhausted men stagger onto the soil they have come to set alight, sucking stalks of cane as they flee inland. The Cuban Revolution begins waist-deep, late, and lost.
stops.quote: We reached solid ground, lost, stumbling along like so many shadows or ghosts marching in response to some obscure psychic impulse.
stops.quote_source: Che Guevara, Reminiscences of the Cuban Revolutionary War

stops.name: Alegría de Pío, the baptism of fire and the choice
stops.campa: Three days inland, betrayed by their guide, the column is resting in a cane field at Alegría de Pío when the army opens fire at point-blank range. In the rout, Che sees at his feet a box of ammunition and a box of medicine, too heavy to carry both. He picks up the ammunition. A bullet tears his neck; blood sheets down and he believes himself dying, remembering a Jack London character composing himself to die with dignity in the snow. He lives. The canon fixes this cane field as the sacrament: the doctor dies at Alegría de Pío, and the soldier is born.
stops.quote: This was perhaps the first time I was faced with the dilemma of choosing between my dedication to medicine and my duty as a revolutionary soldier. At my feet were a pack full of medicine and a case of ammunition; together they were too heavy to carry. I chose the ammunition.
stops.quote_source: Che Guevara, Reminiscences of the Cuban Revolutionary War, 'Alegría de Pío'

stops.name: Cinco Palmas, the regathering of the twelve
stops.campa: Scattered survivors crawl for two weeks through thorn scrub and betrayal, comrades captured and shot along the beaches, toward the farm of Ramón 'Mongo' Pérez at Cinco Palmas. Fidel arrives with two men and asks how many rifles they saved; told seven, he declares that now they have won the war, and the canon records the arithmetic of faith without blinking. Che's group comes in days later, ragged, bringing the number of armed men to roughly a dozen. From these twelve-odd rifles under the palms, the tradition counts the rebirth of the Cuban Revolution, apostolic in its numbers.

stops.name: La Plata, the first victory
stops.campa: Before dawn on the seventeenth of January the reborn guerrilla attacks the small army barracks at the mouth of the La Plata river and takes it: weapons, ammunition, and the news, more valuable than either, that the Rebel Army exists and can win. Che fights as combatant, no longer merely physician. The rebels burn the barracks, treat the enemy wounded courteously and release their prisoners, founding at the first opportunity the code of war that will distinguish them: the wounded soldier of Batista is a future recruit, never a corpse to be made.

stops.name: El Uvero, the coming of age
stops.campa: In open daylight the guerrilla assaults the fortified coastal barracks of El Uvero, eighty rebels against a garrison behind sandbags, and takes it in under three hours of the war's hardest fighting yet. The cost is heavy on both sides. Che the doctor returns for one afternoon: he treats the wounded of both armies, then stays behind with the rebel casualties, guiding them for weeks through the mountains back to the column. The Reminiscences pronounce the verdict the canon repeats: at El Uvero the Rebel Army stopped being fugitives and became a force.
stops.quote: For us this was the victory that marked our coming of age.
stops.quote_source: Che Guevara, Reminiscences of the Cuban Revolutionary War, 'El Uvero'

stops.name: Sierra Maestra, the star of the Comandante
stops.campa: When Fidel constitutes a second column, he gives it to the Argentine. In a letter to Frank País being signed by the officers, Che writes 'Captain' after his name and Fidel says: put Comandante. Celia Sánchez pins to his beret the small star of the rank: the star the whole world will later know from a single photograph. He is the first man raised to comandante after Fidel himself: the foreigner, the asthmatic, the one who chose the ammunition box. The vanity of it delights him, and he confesses the delight in writing, which is why the canon trusts him.
stops.quote: The dose of vanity we all carry within made me feel like the proudest man on earth that day.
stops.quote_source: Che Guevara, Reminiscences of the Cuban Revolutionary War, on his promotion to Comandante

stops.name: El Hombrito, the guerrilla republic
stops.campa: In the valley of El Hombrito, Che's column stops running and starts building: a bread oven, an armory, a shoe workshop, a pig farm, a crude hospital, and a mimeographed newspaper, El Cubano Libre, reviving the name the mambises used against Spain. A tiny hydroelectric dynamo lights the camp. It is the first liberated territory administered by the Revolution, a state the size of a hamlet, run by a man who is discovering that he loves to govern the way he loves to fight: totally, insomniacally, and with a book always open beside the work.

stops.name: El Jíbaro, Column 8 'Ciro Redondo' marches west
stops.campa: Batista's great summer offensive has broken against the Sierra, and Fidel answers with the war's boldest order: two columns will leave the mountains and invade the west, repeating the crossing of the mambí generals Gómez and Maceo in 1895. On the last day of August, Che leads the hundred and forty-odd men of Column 8 'Ciro Redondo' out of El Jíbaro toward Las Villas, five hundred kilometers away across open, garrisoned plain. Camilo Cienfuegos is already ahead of him. The trucks are lost to a storm almost at once; the invasion will walk.

stops.name: The Camagüey plain, the march of hunger and hurricanes
stops.campa: For six weeks the column crosses the flat cattle country of Camagüey in the middle of hurricane season: swamps to the waist, cyclone rains, nothing to eat but raw horse and unsalted meat, feet rotting in ruined boots, the army and the air force pressing every crossing of road and rail. Ambushed at La Federal and again at Cuatro Compañeros, hunted by planes, the men march by night like a procession of mud statues. Che, asthma raging, marches at the head. The canon ranks these weeks with the worst of the whole war: the invasion's forty days in the wilderness.

stops.name: El Pedrero, Escambray, arrival and the mountain pacts
stops.campa: Gaunt as castaways, Column 8 climbs at last into the Escambray mountains of Las Villas, and Che sets up headquarters at the hamlet of El Pedrero. The sierra is crowded with rival guerrillas, the Directorio, the Segundo Frente, feuding chieftains; and the newcomer does with politics what he does with terrain: he unifies it. The Pedrero Pact binds the Directorio's fighters to the Rebel Army for the coming offensive. Here too a young clandestine courier named Aleida March walks into the camp with money taped to her body, and into the rest of his life.

stops.name: Fomento, the first town falls
stops.campa: The December offensive opens: while Batista's elections die of emptiness, Che's column comes down from the Escambray and besieges Fomento, first town of the plan to cut the island in two. After two days the garrison of over a hundred surrenders: the first town liberated in Las Villas, delirious crowds in the streets, rifles passing from the defeated to the barbudos. The method is now doctrine: surround, cut the roads, take the town, free the prisoners, roll to the next junction. The Central Highway, spine of Cuba, lies just ahead.

stops.name: Cabaiguán, the fall from the roof
stops.campa: Guayos and Cabaiguán fall in quick succession as the column reaches the Central Highway itself. Scrambling across a rooftop during the street fighting in Cabaiguán, Che falls from a wall and fractures his left arm; a doctor sets it and the comandante finishes the campaign with his arm in a cast slung in black cloth: the wound the photographs of Santa Clara will show. Six hundred prisoners have been taken in days. He jokes that he is more dangerous to himself than the enemy is. The advance does not pause even one hour for the bones of its commander.
